trans.sense: modify fraudulently to make sth. look better

raw_glosses: (transitive) To make a counterfeit, to counterfeit, to forge, to falsify.
glosses: To make a counterfeit, to counterfeit, to forge, to falsify.

examples.text: "She constantly faked being sick, and perhaps mistakenly, I indulged her more than I should have, pretending I couldn't tell. But I AM a teacher myself, so it's kind of hard to just let this slide."
examples.ref: 2013, Jocelyn Samara D., Rain, volume 1, →ISBN, page 193:

raw_glosses: (transitive) To make a false display of, to affect, to feign, to simulate.
glosses: To make a false display of, to affect, to feign, to simulate.

raw_glosses: (archaic) To cheat; to swindle; to steal; to rob.
glosses: To cheat; to swindle; to steal; to rob.

examples.text: He had a hundred similar tricks, but I never knew him fake a horse, or sell one as sound if it was not.

raw_glosses: (archaic) To modify fraudulently, so as to make an object appear better or other than it really is
glosses: To modify fraudulently, so as to make an object appear better or other than it really is

examples.text: Occasionally the opportunity arises to stand up and "fake" a jazz standard.
In the face of this print music culture, 'faking' was the ability—at once respected and disrespected—to improvise a song (or a part in an arrangement) without reading the notation.
examples.ref: Denning, cited in 2020, Matt Brennan, Kick It: A Social History of the Drum Kit (page 110)

raw_glosses: (Islam) A religious mendicant who owns no personal property.
glosses: A religious mendicant who owns no personal property.

examples.text: The preposterous altruism too![…]Resist not evil. It is an insane immolation of self—as bad intrinsically as fakirs stabbing themselves or anchorites warping their spines in caves scarcely large enough for a fair-sized dog.
examples.ref: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter XVI, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:

raw_glosses: (Hinduism, more loosely) An ascetic mendicant, especially one who performs feats of endurance or apparent magic.
glosses: An ascetic mendicant, especially one who performs feats of endurance or apparent magic.

examples.text: He denounces no one until he has all the damaging facts in hand, very frequently backed up with affidavits. He 'Lawsonized' certain stock jobbers and financial fakirs of London before the Boston advertising man was heard of.

examples.text: "But a stranger who had come up to the group just at this point, when they were pronouncing the soup delicious, laughed aloud. "'What a set of fools you all are!' he cried. 'This tramp is just a fakir. That stone had nothing to do with the soup."
He was, as the undercover agent concluded, a fabulous raconteur or, as one other person summed him up, "a monumental fakir and liar."

glosses: Someone who takes advantage of the gullible through fakery, especially of a spiritual or religious nature.
